The Quantum Catch-22 and the LCAO Lifeline

Welcome to the reality of quantum mechanics: the Schrödinger equation is our catch-all master equation that tells us everything there is to know about a molecule. But there’s a catch. If we try to solve the Schrödinger equation in its raw differential form, things get out of hand really, really quickly.

For any realistic molecule with multiple atoms and multiple electrons, the differential equation gets overwhelmed by all the potential energy terms. It was already pretty bad with just two protons and one electron (three potential energy terms). Add one more electron, and the number of terms blows up to six. By the time you get to benzene or diamond, it becomes practically unsolvable.

So, we take a better approach. We give up on solving the differential equation exactly. Instead, we guess what the solution (the wavefunction) will look like using known building blocks. This is the Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO). We assume that the atomic wavefunctions we know (like from the hydrogen atom) will apply to other atoms as well. It’s a simplification, but it works incredibly well.

By doing this, we transform a god-awful differential equation into a much more tractable matrix equation: \begin{equation} \hat{H} \psi = E \psi \implies \begin{pmatrix} H_{11} & H_{12} \\ H_{21} & H_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} = E \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} \tag{1} \end{equation} Here, \hat{H} is the Hamiltonian operator (now a matrix), \psi is our wavefunction (represented by the vector of coefficients c_i), and E represents the allowed energy levels (the eigenvalues). The diagonal elements (H_{11}, H_{22}) are the self-energies of an electron at an isolated atom, which we call -\alpha. The off-diagonal elements (H_{12}, H_{21}) represent the interaction or coupling between different atomic sites, which we call -\beta. Both \alpha and \beta are typically on the order of 1\text{ eV} (electron volt), which is our go-to unit of energy in this class.

Recap: Molecular Orbitals of \text{H}_2

In your homework, you solved this 2 \times 2 matrix equation for the hydrogen molecule (\text{H}_2). Because it’s a 2 \times 2 matrix, we expect two eigenvalues (energies) and two corresponding eigenvectors (wavefunctions).

The Bonding Orbital (Lower Energy)

The lower energy eigenvalue is: \begin{equation} E_{\text{bond}} = -\alpha - \beta \tag{2} \end{equation} The corresponding eigenvector tells us the shape of the orbital. You might be tempted to write the eigenvector as \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, and while that’s technically a valid eigenvector, it’s not normalized. The length of that vector is \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}. We prefer our eigenvectors to have a length of exactly 1. So, we divide by the length to get the normalized eigenvector: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \tag{3} \end{equation} These coefficients c_1 and c_2 are the weights for our building blocks. The total wavefunction for the bonding orbital is: \begin{equation} \psi_{\text{bond}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\psi_1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\psi_2 \tag{4} \end{equation} Physically, this means the two atomic wavefunctions (which look like little pointy hats) overlap and add together constructively. We are highly likely to find the electron sitting right between the two protons.

The Antibonding Orbital (Higher Energy)

The higher energy eigenvalue is: \begin{equation} E_{\text{antibond}} = -\alpha + \beta \tag{5} \end{equation} The normalized eigenvector for this state has opposite signs for the two components: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \tag{6} \end{equation} (Note: \begin{pmatrix} -1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} is also fine; flipping the signs globally doesn’t change the physics). This gives us the antibonding wavefunction: \begin{equation} \psi_{\text{antibond}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\psi_1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\psi_2 \tag{7} \end{equation} Attaching a negative sign to one of the atomic wavefunctions flips it upside down. When they overlap, they cancel out in the middle, creating a node—a location where you will never, ever find an electron.

Here is a general truth in quantum mechanics: more nodes mean higher energy. As we go to higher and higher energy molecular orbitals, you are going to see a lot more nodes.

If you were looking at a brand new molecular orbital and saw it had three nodes, would you expect it to have a higher or lower energy than an orbital with only one node?

You would expect it to have a higher energy! In quantum mechanics, more nodes mean the wavefunction is wiggling more rapidly, which translates to higher kinetic energy for the electron. So, a three-node orbital sits higher on the energy ladder than a one-node orbital.

Hybridized Orbitals and the \pi Bond

Now, let’s apply this LCAO concept to more complicated molecules, specifically hydrocarbons. In general chemistry, you probably talked about "hybridized" orbitals. Mathematically, hybridization is exactly what we’ve been doing: a linear combination of atomic orbitals.

Let’s look at the valence electrons in a carbon atom. They live in the 2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, and 2p_z orbitals.

Saturated Hydrocarbons (\text{sp}^3)

A saturated carbon atom has exactly four single bonds sticking out of it (like in ethane, \text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_3). It is "maxed out"—you can’t squeeze any more bonds onto it. The atomic orbitals mix to form an \text{sp}^3 hybridized orbital, which is a linear combination of all four valence orbitals: \begin{equation} \psi_{\text{sp}^3} = a_1[2s] + a_2[2p_x] + a_3[2p_y] + a_4[2p_z] \tag{8} \end{equation} To ensure the wavefunction is normalized, the coefficients must satisfy: \begin{equation} \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2 + a_4^2} = 1 \tag{9} \end{equation}

Unsaturated Hydrocarbons (\text{sp}^2) and the \pi Bond

An unsaturated carbon atom has only three things sticking out of it (a double bond counts as one connection). A classic example is ethylene (or ethene), \text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2. Here, the carbon is \text{sp}^2 hybridized, meaning we only mix the 2s orbital and two of the p orbitals (let’s say 2p_x and 2p_y): \begin{equation} \psi_{\text{sp}^2} = b_1[2s] + b_2[2p_x] + b_3[2p_y] \tag{10} \end{equation}

But wait, we left somebody out! The 2p_z orbital is still hanging out, sticking up vertically from the plane of the molecule. When two neighboring unsaturated carbon atoms bring their leftover 2p_z orbitals together, they overlap side-to-side to form a \pi bond.

The \pi bond is the star of our lesson today. It sits a little higher in energy than the \sigma (single) bonds, and the electrons in the \pi bond are highly delocalized. They can easily hop from one carbon site to the next. If you want to make organic electronic devices, you rely on this electron conduction within the \pi bonds.

Mathematically, the \pi molecular orbital is just another linear combination, this time combining the 2p_z orbital from the first carbon and the 2p_z orbital from the second carbon: \begin{equation} \psi_{\pi} = c_1[2p_{z,1}] + c_2[2p_{z,2}] \tag{11} \end{equation}

The Hückel Model: Step-by-Step

LCAO is like building a house out of bricks. Or, culturally speaking, I might say I’m a linear combination of America and Japan—some weighted sum of my experiences.

The Hückel model is a specific, highly simplified type of LCAO used exclusively for conjugated hydrocarbons—molecules with alternating single and double bonds. In this model, we ignore the \sigma bonds (the \text{sp}^2 framework) and focus entirely on the leftover 2p_z orbitals that form the \pi network.

Let’s apply the Hückel model to a linear chain molecule: 1,3,5-hexatriene (\text{C}_6\text{H}_8).

Step 1: Count the Unsaturated Carbon Atoms

First, we figure out how many carbon atoms in the molecule are unsaturated. Looking at 1,3,5-hexatriene, every single carbon atom has exactly three bonds sticking out of it (one double bond and two single bonds). Therefore, all 6 carbon atoms are unsaturated. \begin{equation} N = 6 \tag{12} \end{equation} This number N tells us exactly how big our Hamiltonian matrix will be. We are going to build a 6 \times 6 matrix.

Step 2: Construct the Hamiltonian Matrix

A 6 \times 6 matrix has 36 elements, which sounds like a pain to deal with. But the beauty of the Hückel model is that it drastically simplifies the interactions. There are only two pillars to this model:

  1. Self-Energy: We care about the energy of an electron sitting on its own 2p_z orbital.

  2. Nearest-Neighbor Interaction: We only care about the interaction between a carbon atom and its immediate next-door neighbors. We pretend all other atoms don’t exist.

Let’s translate these rules into matrix elements H_{ij}:

Diagonal Elements (i = j): These represent the self-energy of each carbon’s 2p_z orbital. We set all diagonal elements to -\alpha. The negative sign indicates that the isolated atomic orbital is a stable state. \begin{equation} H_{11} = H_{22} = H_{33} = H_{44} = H_{55} = H_{66} = -\alpha \tag{13} \end{equation}

Nearest-Neighbor Elements (|i - j| = 1): These represent the interaction energy between adjacent carbons. For example, carbon 1 is bonded to carbon 2, so H_{12} and H_{21} are nearest neighbors. Carbon 2 is bonded to 1 and 3, so H_{23} and H_{32} are nearest neighbors. We set all nearest-neighbor interactions to -\beta. \begin{equation} H_{ij} = -\beta \quad \text{if } i \text{ and } j \text{ are adjacent} \tag{14} \end{equation}

All Other Elements: If two carbons are not immediate neighbors (e.g., carbon 1 and carbon 3), we ignore their interaction. \begin{equation} H_{ij} = 0 \quad \text{if } i \text{ and } j \text{ are not adjacent} \tag{15} \end{equation}

Putting it all together, our 6 \times 6 Hückel matrix for 1,3,5-hexatriene looks like this: \begin{equation} \tag{16} H = \begin{pmatrix} -\alpha & -\beta & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -\beta & -\alpha & -\beta & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\beta & -\alpha & -\beta & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\beta & -\alpha & -\beta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -\beta & -\alpha & -\beta \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -\beta & -\alpha \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} Notice the pattern? We have -\alpha straight down the main diagonal, -\beta on the two sub-diagonals right next to it, and big fat zeros everywhere else.

If we were building this matrix for a shorter linear chain like 1,3-butadiene (C_4H_6), what would the dimensions of the matrix be, and how many -\beta terms would be in the first row?

The matrix would be 4 \times 4 because there are four unsaturated carbon atoms. The first row would only have a single -\beta term at the H_{12} position, because carbon 1 is only bonded to carbon 2. The rest of the row would just be zeros, keeping things nice and simple!

Step 3: Solve the Eigenvalue Equation

Our ultimate goal is to solve the eigenvalue equation: \begin{equation} \hat{H} \ket{\psi} = E \ket{\psi} \tag{17} \end{equation} Or, written out with our matrix and coefficient vector: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} -\alpha & -\beta & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -\beta & -\alpha & -\beta & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\beta & -\alpha & -\beta & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\beta & -\alpha & -\beta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -\beta & -\alpha & -\beta \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -\beta & -\alpha \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3 \\ c_4 \\ c_5 \\ c_6 \end{pmatrix} = E \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3 \\ c_4 \\ c_5 \\ c_6 \end{pmatrix} \tag{18} \end{equation} Solving a 6 \times 6 matrix by hand is a nightmare, so we won’t do it. In your homework, you will use a computer program to find the six allowed energy levels (E) and the six corresponding eigenvectors (c_1 through c_6). The eigenvectors will tell us the shapes of the six different \pi molecular orbitals for hexatriene.

Looking Ahead: Benzene

Next time, we will apply the Hückel model to a molecule that isn’t just a linear chain: benzene (\text{C}_6\text{H}_6).

Benzene also has 6 unsaturated carbons, so it will also have a 6 \times 6 matrix. However, because it forms a ring, carbon 1 is now bonded to carbon 6! I want you to think about how that nearest-neighbor interaction between site 1 and site 6 will change the look of the matrix we just built. We’ll work through it together in class.

Based on our rules for the Hückel matrix, what specific matrix elements H_{ij} will change from 0 to -\beta when we switch from linear hexatriene to ring-shaped benzene?

The elements H_{16} and H_{61} will change to -\beta. In the linear chain, carbons 1 and 6 were far apart, so their interaction was zero. In the benzene ring, they are now next-door neighbors, so we have to plug in our coupling energy at those top-right and bottom-left corners of the matrix.
